# Key Concepts for Epidemiologists & Microbiologists {#sec-concepts}

This chapter explains the science PhyloTrace implements, in plain language. It is
the reference the later chapters point back to: when @sec-mst describes the
controls of the minimum spanning tree, this is where "what a minimum spanning
tree *is*" was explained. Read it once and the rest of the manual reads more
easily.

## From an assembly to an allele profile {#sec-concepts-assembly}

### Whole-genome assemblies

The starting point is a **whole-genome assembly**: the reconstructed DNA
sequence of one bacterial isolate, produced by sequencing its genome and
stitching the reads into contiguous stretches ("contigs"). In PhyloTrace an
assembly is a FASTA file (`.fasta`, `.fa` or `.fna`), and it is the *only*
input the workflow needs (@sec-typing).

### Loci, alleles and the core genome

A **locus** (plural *loci*) is a defined position in the genome — in practice a
specific gene. An **allele** is one observed DNA sequence at that locus. Two
isolates carry the *same* allele at a locus when their sequence there is
identical, and *different* alleles when it differs by even a single base.

The **core genome** is the set of loci present in essentially all members of a
species. **Core-genome MLST (cgMLST)** types an isolate by reading its allele at
every locus in a standardized core-genome scheme — typically 1,500–3,000 loci —
and recording *which* allele it carries at each. This generalizes classical
**MLST** [@maiden1998mlst], which used only ~7 housekeeping genes.

::: {.callout-tip title="Concept — why alleles instead of raw DNA differences?"}
cgMLST records only *whether* two alleles differ, not *how much*. A locus is
either the same allele or a different one; a one-base change and a fifty-base
change both count as "different." This discards information relative to raw
sequence comparison, but it is what makes results **portable and stable**:
every lab that types the same isolate against the same scheme gets the same
allele call, so allele numbers can be compared across labs, instruments and
years — which raw SNP counts, sensitive to read depth and alignment, cannot.
It is the same logic that made 7-gene MLST a *portable* method
[@maiden1998mlst], scaled up to the whole core genome.
:::

### Allele profiles and sequence types

An isolate's **allele profile** is the vector of its allele calls — one entry
per locus. It corresponds to a row in a table with isolates as rows, loci as
columns, and each cell holding an allele identifier.

A **sequence type (ST)** is a name for a profile that has been seen before and
registered in a nomenclature. In classical 7-gene MLST every distinct
combination of the 7 alleles gets an ST number; PhyloTrace resolves these
against public repositories (@sec-typing). At cgMLST resolution, profiles are so
specific that most are unique, so relatedness is judged by *distance* between
profiles rather than by shared ST names.

::: {.callout-important title="Allele numbers are local; allele *content* is universal"}
PhyloTrace gives every distinct allele sequence two identities: a short local
number, convenient inside one database, and a **content fingerprint** derived
from the DNA sequence itself. Only the fingerprint is meaningful outside the file
— two databases will assign different numbers to the same allele simply because
they encountered it at different times. This is why comparing or merging
databases always works from the fingerprint (@sec-concepts-hashing,
@sec-interop), and why an allele number you see in one database should never be
quoted to a colleague working in another.
:::

## Measuring relatedness: allelic distance {#sec-concepts-distance}

### The Hamming distance

Given two allele profiles, their **allelic distance** is simply the number of
loci at which they carry different alleles. This is the **Hamming distance**
[@hamming1950]: count the mismatching columns. Two isolates that differ at 3 of
2,000 loci are 3 apart; two that differ at 800 are 800 apart.

::: {.callout-tip title="Concept — distance as a proxy for time and transmission"}
Bacteria accumulate genetic change roughly with time and replication, so a
*small* allelic distance between two isolates indicates a very recent common
ancestor — consistent with direct transmission or a common source — while a
*large* distance indicates divergence long ago. Allelic distance is therefore
the quantitative basis of outbreak analysis: it converts the question of
relatedness between isolates into a number that can be thresholded, clustered
and plotted.
:::

### The missing-data problem

Real assemblies do not always yield a clean call at every locus: a locus may be
absent, fragmented across contigs, or fail quality thresholds, leaving a
**missing** value. How you treat missing calls when comparing two profiles
changes the distance, so PhyloTrace makes the policy explicit. Three options are
offered:

| Policy | Rule | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| **Ignore missing** (`ignore_na`) | Compare only loci called in *both* isolates | Default; robust to patchy assemblies |
| **Missing as category** (`category`) | "missing" is itself a value: missing vs called counts as a difference, missing vs missing does not | When absence is biologically meaningful |
| **Omit loci** (`omit`) | Drop any locus missing in *any* isolate, then compare the rest | Strictest; a common column set for all |

The choice appears as the **NA handling** control on every distance-based plot,
and the same policy feeds both the tree and the MST, so the two views of one
dataset always agree about how far apart two isolates are (@sec-mst, @sec-trees).

## Minimum spanning trees {#sec-concepts-mst}

### What a minimum spanning tree is

Represent each isolate as a node, and every pair of isolates as a potential edge
whose length is their allelic distance. A **spanning tree** connects all nodes
with edges such that everything is joined and no loops form. The **minimum**
spanning tree (MST) is the spanning tree whose total edge length is smallest —
the most economical set of connections that still links every isolate
[@prim1957; @kruskal1956].

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-concepts-mst
%%| fig-cap: "A minimum spanning tree over five isolates. Edge numbers are allelic distances; the MST keeps the cheapest set of links that connects all nodes."
flowchart LR
  A((A)) ---|2| B((B))
  B ---|3| C((C))
  B ---|1| D((D))
  D ---|4| E((E))
```

### Why epidemiologists use them

For allelic-profile data the MST has become the standard representation for
outbreak analysis, popularized by goeBURST and PHYLOViZ
[@francisco2009goeburst; @nascimento2017phyloviz]. It offers three properties
that make it well suited to this use:

- **Every isolate is a visible node** — unlike a phylogenetic tree, where
  isolates sit at the tips and internal branch points are hypothetical
  ancestors, the MST draws the *actual* isolates and joins the closest ones.
- **Edge labels are directly interpretable** — "these two isolates differ by
  2 alleles" is written on the line between them.
- **Clusters are visually distinct** — tightly-linked groups (say, all within
  10 alleles) form dense subgraphs, and a threshold turns them into named
  clusters.

::: {.callout-important title="Identical isolates share a node"}
Before the tree is drawn, isolates that are **zero alleles apart** are merged
into a single node — chains of identical profiles collapse together — and that
node is drawn larger to show how many isolates it stands for. So a "node" in a
PhyloTrace MST is a *set* of indistinguishable isolates, not necessarily one
isolate, and the count matters when you read cluster sizes off the plot
(@sec-mst).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Concept — the MST is a summary, not a proven history"}
An MST shows *one* cheapest way to connect the isolates. When several links are
tied, the choice among them is arbitrary, and the MST cannot represent
reticulation (a bacterium's history is not always tree-shaped). It provides an
accurate summary of pairwise closeness, useful for identifying clusters and
plausible transmission chains, but it is not a proven genealogy.
:::

## Phylogenetic trees {#sec-concepts-trees}

Where the MST connects the observed isolates directly, a **phylogenetic tree**
reconstructs a branching genealogy: isolates sit at the tips, and internal
branch points represent inferred common ancestors. PhyloTrace builds trees from
the same allelic distance matrix, using two classic algorithms with different
assumptions.

### Neighbour-Joining (NJ)

**Neighbour-Joining** [@saitou1987nj] builds the tree by repeatedly joining the
pair of isolates that are closest *after* correcting for how far each is from
everything else. It does **not** assume a constant rate of change, so branch
lengths can vary freely — a fast-evolving lineage gets a long branch. This makes
NJ a good default for showing structure without imposing a clock.

### UPGMA

**UPGMA** [@sokal1958upgma] joins the closest clusters and places their common
ancestor at their average distance, assuming a roughly **constant rate of
change** (a molecular clock). The result is an *ultrametric* tree — every tip
ends level, at the same distance from the root — which represents nested
clustering directly but can misrepresent relationships when lineages evolve at
different rates.

::: {.callout-tip title="Concept — choosing between UPGMA and Neighbour-Joining"}
Use **UPGMA** for a hierarchical clustering representation when the isolates
are expected to evolve at similar rates. Use **Neighbour-Joining** when some
lineages may be more divergent than others and should not be forced level. If
the two trees disagree substantially, the disagreement is itself informative:
it usually indicates uneven rates of change, in which case NJ is the more
reliable interpretation.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Branch lengths are allele differences, in every view"}
Both trees are built from the *same* distances the MST uses — raw allele
differences — so a pair shown "3272 apart" reads identically wherever you look at
it. Neighbour-Joining can occasionally compute a very slightly negative branch,
which has no biological meaning; those are set to zero, the standard fix, rather
than the whole tree being rescaled. Whether a branch is long enough to have its
number *printed* on it is a separate, purely visual decision (@sec-trees).
:::

## Antimicrobial resistance, virulence and stress markers {#sec-concepts-amr}

Beyond relatedness, PhyloTrace screens each assembly for **genes of clinical
interest**: acquired antimicrobial-resistance (AMR) determinants, virulence
factors, and stress/biocide/metal-tolerance elements. This uses NCBI's
**AMRFinderPlus** [@feldgarden2021amrfinderplus] through the curation wrapper
**abritamr** [@sherry2023abritamr] (@sec-amr).

::: {.callout-tip title="Concept — what an 'AMR determinant' is, and is not"}
A detected AMR gene means the isolate *carries a sequence known to confer, or
contribute to, resistance* to a drug class. It is a **genotype**, not a measured
phenotype: it does not by itself prove the isolate is clinically resistant
(expression, regulation and combinations matter). For point mutations —
resistance caused by a single base change in a core gene rather than an acquired
gene — AMRFinderPlus can only call them when it knows the organism, which is why
PhyloTrace passes the scheme's species where the tool supports it and silently
falls back where it does not.
:::

PhyloTrace keeps two complementary views of the result: a **granular** one with
one entry per detected element, and a **curated per-isolate roll-up** by drug
class. The heatmaps in @sec-amr-heatmap read both back to show presence/absence
across isolates, alongside the same metadata used to annotate trees and maps.

## Epidemic curves {#sec-concepts-epi}

An **epidemic curve** (epi curve) plots the number of cases against their date
of collection, and is among the oldest methods used in outbreak investigation.
Its shape distinguishes a point-source outbreak (a sharp peak) from
person-to-person spread (successive waves) and shows when an outbreak began
and whether it is waning.

::: {.callout-important title="Reading a PhyloTrace epi curve"}
Collection dates are binned into intervals (day, week, month…) chosen to keep the
number of bars readable; the vertical axis counts whole cases, so it carries only
integer ticks; and every bar is exactly one interval wide. That last point
matters when you read the plot: **a gap in the curve is a genuine gap in the
data**, not a drawing artefact. Cases can be stratified and coloured by any
metadata field or custom variable (@sec-epicurve).
:::

## Content hashing: identity that travels {#sec-concepts-hashing}

Two labs can only compare or merge data if they agree on what counts as "the
same" allele and "the same" isolate. PhyloTrace secures both with cryptographic
hashing.

- **Allele identity.** Every allele is identified by a cryptographic hash of its
  DNA sequence. The same sequence hashes to the same value wherever it is
  computed, so two databases can recognise a shared allele **by content**, with
  no shared numbering scheme. This is what makes merging databases safe
  (@sec-interop), and it is the same approach chewBBACA takes with its hash-based
  profiles [@silva2018chewbbaca].
- **Assembly identity.** Every typed assembly is fingerprinted with a GA4GH-style
  sequence digest [@ga4gh_refget] and the fingerprint is stored against the
  isolate. A match proves two typing runs consumed the byte-identical assembly; a
  mismatch proves nothing, so PhyloTrace uses it to *flag* a possible duplicate
  and never to block work (@sec-typing).

::: {.callout-tip title="Concept — why a hash is better than a name"}
Names are fragile: renaming an assembly file and re-typing it creates a second,
unrelated isolate record in a naive system; giving two different assemblies the
same name silently merges them into one. A **content hash** ignores names
entirely and evaluates only whether the underlying sequence is identical. This
is what allows PhyloTrace databases to be copied, renamed, exported and
re-imported across labs while still agreeing, byte-for-byte, on which alleles
and assemblies are genuinely shared.
:::
